utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could we call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. And this is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Anna Richterova, and Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic, my co-counsel, and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suppose -- good afternoon to you. I suppose -- I would suggest to you to ask Mr. Rohde to furnish your co-counsel with some kind of a bag which is not an Albert Heijn one. Yes. I understand that there are some preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I wanted to show you these tapes that are sitting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is about half of the tapes from the Stakic case that my client has to listen to. They are -- they're roughly two hours each. Just for one witness, there are 12 of them. It will take him 24 hours just to listen to one witness in this. There are some more over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I -- Usher, could you bring me one of those tapes, please. These are all 90-minute tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was looking at those. These are all 120s. I assumed they were all the same. You're right. These are 90s. But these are all 120s. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, now, when you sit down, please work it out and give me the total number of hours. What I would also like to know -- usually -- I mean, the technicians should be in a position to tell me this. When we see a tape like that, I understand that bundle that you showed me that -- are in -- tied with a rubber band because they refer to the same witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. This would be one witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be one witness. So I would presume that those tapes with perhaps the last tape would be full, complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't want to represent that the tapes are all completely full and I certainly don't have time to listen to them so see that they are. But I assume that they use them with some efficiency and put as much on them as they can before--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But once you have finished with this submission I would like you to sit down and perhaps you or one of your colleagues could work out what were talking about precisely -- to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have to -- I have quite a stack of them at my office too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, as well. These were just -- these, I got today. Those are part of the ones that we got last week. But these were just delivered today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't see the others because they are hidden behind the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, these -- these are all 120s here, so that's the stack there. In addition, Your Honour, since -- since we were in court last Thursday, I think I have received -- and I -- I tell you that I have not wasted time counting pages, but I think that we've received an additional discovery material regarding the Prijedor phase of this case about another 3.000 pages. The estimate that you heard Thursday, that the material that I had to deal with was around 2500 pages was just wildly wrong. One witness is nearly 2500 pages, just one of the witnesses all by himself. The Registry allows in terms of payment two minutes per page for reading material. And as you know, mere reading is not what I do. I have to prepare a cross-examination. So not only do I have to read the material, but then I have to compare it with other material and go through that process of preparing cross, which I suggest to you probably takes a little more than two minutes per page. Maybe not a lot, because I actually read faster than two minutes a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And some pages you skim through obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But if you just figure it out at two minutes per page, on the material that we've received since last Thursday, it's a hundred hours work, and that's all new stuff that we didn't have when I spoke to you on Thursday about the problem. I think -- and all I can do is give you the best estimate. There are -- I know that in all of the witness material that we have, there are approximately 40.000 pages of material, because it's scanned and the computer tells me how many pages are in there. Prijedor, I think, represents about 25 per cent of that. So if that's correct, there are about 10.000 pages of Prijedor material plus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But what I am more interested in, Mr. Ackerman, is the new material, what you have had for the past months, please don't include in this whole presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the new material, Your Honour, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is Stakic. The new material is primarily Stakic and exhibits associated with Stakic. And that's going to represent with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again, but I suppose that some, if not most, of the material presented in Stakic was already in your possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very recently. It -- I haven't had it -- I haven't had much of it very long. Some of it we've had for a while, but a lot of it has just been provided to us recently. And today there is this that was handed. This is additional Prijedor material. In my locker downstairs there are two envelopes this thick that I understand are additional Prijedor material. And, you know, Your Honour, if it was 2500 pages, like you may have thought last Thursday, I wouldn't have a thing in the world to complain about. But it's a great deal more than that -- I mean a really great deal more than that. And when you are handed the transcripts for Witness 7.45, it -- it took me four days to read those. And I went through -- I was doing it and making notes at the time, so you'll get through it faster than four days, but it will take you two or three, I bet. They're huge. This material is just overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Ms. Korner in the building or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner won't be here till Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are some things that I'm going to propose. Number one is a meeting early next week with Mr. Rohde. This will be in my Chambers, for you Mr. Ackerman, for Ms. Korner, and Mr. Rohde from the office. Be prepared -- and I will convene the meeting once you have more or less articulated this out, and be in a position to present it in a way that makes a case. Right? Then I promise you my help. That, I suppose, should be held -- that meeting should be held when Ms. Korner is here, because I suppose -- no offence meant to either of you, but I think she is more familiar with the -- what has been disclosed and handed over. If you are, then tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, I am pretty well familiar with what was disclosed, because I am the person responsible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In charge of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Not in charge of Prijedor but generally for disclosure, so I am familiar with material which was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- that's even better. So I will combine my skills of a diplomat with those of a jurist and suggest to you that between now and when we have this meeting, please find time to sit down together. I want you to be honest with each other and together with the Trial Chamber, who can then help both of you to make sure that this is a fair trial. What I would like you to do is: Mr. Ackerman will sort out what he has to deal with. He and his colleagues, plus then what his client has to deal with, because if these are tapes that Mr. Brdjanin has to listen to, then obviously we have to take that into consideration. It doesn't mean to say that I would expect him to listen to all those tapes before we move. We will take it as we go along one witness after the other. And therefore, we would need to plan accordingly. But if the number of hours that are being made available payment-wise to the Defence team is not sufficient, then we will have to do something about it and we will intervene. However, we will need and require from you a properly articulated statement indicating exactly what is involved here before we can make any representations ourselves. As far as you are concerned, Madam Richterova, what I would like you to do is to sit down with Mr. Ackerman and then come back to us explaining exactly what was disclosed and when. We are particularly interested in the volume of recent disclosures, recent disclosures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It can be done very easily because we have records of all our disclosures with dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So what I would like from you is this: That we have a list of witnesses for Prijedor, and starting with -- forget the next one, because the next one I would imagine we will start with today. No? Or today or tomorrow. So forget the next one, the 7.178. Start with 7.185. And you go down chronologically or -- as you have presented them in this order of witnesses, which is dated 15th of October. If you are revising this, then please refer to a revised version. What I would like you to do is this: 7.185, then what I would like is information as to when the supporting material was disclosed. If this is going to be a Rule 92 witness, for example, because this person may have given testimony, evidence, in Stakic or in some other case, then please indicate -- I know that Ms. Gustin is going to have to do this probably. No? Please indicate to me that this is going to be a Rule 92 -- material for Rule 92 was disclosed on such and such a day, and it involves two tapes, three tapes, 100 pages, 200 page, 1.000 pages, et cetera. Because if, as Mr. Ackerman suggested, there is one witness, for example, whose testimony runs into -- into thousands -- did I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the material for one of the witnesses, Your Honour, exceeds 2.000 pages. But I really want to emphasise that I'm just guessing, because I have not counted the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to make that really clear to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, I can quite understand that there could be problems, but I want to make sure that if there is a problem, what is the extent of this problem. And then we will sit together, if necessary, in public session, if necessary, and with Mr. Rohde privately in my chambers to see exactly how best to proceed. And then we will report later on in an open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will tell you that I -- that I actually had a meeting with Mr. Rohde about this problem and the hours that it was going to require, and he told me that he would -- he would likely approve up to 175 out-of-court hours a month. I will tell you that I am at 245 for this month right now, so I hunch that I am here as a volunteer for the United Nations and I'm not particularly willing to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't expect any monuments or any medals, Mr. Ackerman. You will -- I never got any and you won't get any. So let's leave it at that for the time being. I think you do a bit of homework, taking some of these 245 hours that you probably are -- that are probably haunting you. I'm pretty sure that Madam Richterova and her colleagues are going to find the time too, to outline this for me, and then we will plan accordingly. What I can promise you is that we will try to make some sense out of this apparent mess. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just clarify a couple of things. In relation to the page length that Mr. Ackerman gave, 2.500, that Ms. Korner spoke about last week. That figure, I think, she got from myself and that was in answer to a question as to the amount of material that we will be submitting to the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we asked the same question ourselves, and that was what we were told. That was even before the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. But that was me working out on the assumption that we were going to submit one transcript because that was what had been decided -- one transcript for each of these witnesses who had -- may have testified in multiple trials previously. And so of course that figure would then balloon out, because I spoke with Mr. Ackerman yesterday and he wants every transcript -- prior transcript of the witnesses to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. And of course that wasn't my understanding when I gave Ms. Korner the figure last week. So I just wanted to clarify that point. Also, just if I may, before we deal with it in -- next week, just in relation to the Prijedor evidence, obviously most of the disclosure will have been recent because the Stakic trial only began in April and only finished in September. And I think for the majority of the witnesses, once we obtain permission from the Court, which was on an going basis, we disclosed the hard copy of the transcripts. Obviously the tapes have only recently been disclosed because they've just only been finished by the people who have been listening to them. And in relation to the witness list, there is going to be a change in the order of witnesses and we were going to provide Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman with a new list on Thursday once we had confirmation of a change in the order. We are trying to accommodate Mr. Ackerman's request that we don't have two big witnesses back to back, and so we contacted two witnesses yesterday and asked if they would swap. And after we got that confirmation, today or tomorrow we were going to provide an updated list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And what I want you to understand, and I'm pretty sure you understand it very clearly, is that the system -- these trials in this Tribunal proceed is pretty much unique. It's completely different to what we are used to at home. I mean, the factor of ongoing disclosure in the course of the trial and ongoing disclosures of the extent and of the volume that we are talking about, when we are supposed to start hearing and when we have actually started hearing the evidence in that particular municipality is of concern. It's -- you ought to compare it with an ordinary trial by jury or whatever in your own jurisdiction where all of a sudden a new document comes up, a simple new document. If the Defence is taken by surprise or if the Prosecution is taken by surprise, usually you ask for time and time is granted. That's no major big deal in an ordinary trial in our jurisdiction. But over here it can create big problems. And I want to make sure when I go to bed, to sleep at night, that I go to sleep with my conscience clear, knowing that I am, together with my two colleagues, conducting a fair trial. If I have doubts, any doubts, I will stop. All right? So that is the -- that is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me add one more thing: The Chamber needs to know that the Prosecution and I are working together trying to make this thing work. I suppose I've talked with Ms. Sutherland two or three times a day since Saturday about various matters. And what you just heard from her is an example of what we're trying to do to make it work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They had scheduled two very, very large witnesses that requires huge preparation back to back, and that would have caused me to ask you for time, and I suggested that if they separated those two witnesses, that we could probably work through it and not have to do that. And they agreed and as you just heard they're trying to accomplish that. So please understand, the Trial Chamber, that we are both working to make this happen. And I don't think anybody here is trying to thwart the continuation of this case. We're trying to keep it going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't cross my mind. I mean at no time did I suggest that I was suspecting that. I hope that you have not understood in any case -- in any way that I was hinting at that. I'm pretty sure, as I have always stated -- I'm pretty convinced of the good faith and well-meaning of both of you. So can we bring in the witness now. Yes. We'll go into closed session first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.37 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
